clinicalPearls: Poisoning severity is dose-related, but individual responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphisms, enzyme induction or inhibition from co-ingested xenobiotics, and acquired tolerance; the functional reserve of the target organ (influenced by age and preexisting disease) also shapes severity and reversibility.

Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first characterize the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a toxidrome and finally for agent-specific clues.

Core temperature must be measured and reassessed frequently even in combative patients, because temperature elevation is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning (e.g., cocaine) and in withdrawal states (e.g., alcohol, GHB).

Mydriasis is characteristic of all stimulant states but is most marked in anticholinergic poisoning because pupillary reactivity is muscarinic; sympathomimetic poisoning also dilates pupils but some light reactivity persists, whereas the anticholinergic toxidrome adds hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds, and urinary retention.
Rotatory nystagmus points specifically to phencyclidine or ketamine, the only physiologic stimulants that produce this sign.
Miosis is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning; cholinergic poisoning is distinguished by accompanying muscarinic and nicotinic features.

A normal exam can be deceptive: 'toxic time-bombs' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism) and the proliferation of once-daily extended-release formulations mean delayed, severe toxicity is increasingly common.

A rapid response to a diagnostic antidote can confirm the cause: improvement within minutes of IV dextrose, naloxone, or flumazenil is essentially diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning, and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively.

Qualitative urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only: false positives and negatives are common (e.g., fluoroquinolones cause false-positive opiate screens), and newer agents such as synthetic cannabinoids (spice), cathinones (bath salts), and kratom are not detected at all.
Symptomatic patients (e.g., apnea from opioids) should be managed on the basis of history, examination, and the observed toxidrome without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

Effects after overdose typically begin sooner, peak later, and last longer than after a therapeutic dose, and the toxicokinetic profile differs from the published therapeutic pharmacokinetics in standard references.

Most patients who are asymptomatic 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and can be discharged safely, but longer observation is mandatory after suspected toxic time-bomb ingestions.
harrison.pathophysiology: Poisoning is the development of dose-related adverse effects from exposure to chemicals, drugs, or other xenobiotics. Effects may be local (skin, eyes, lungs) or systemic depending on the route of exposure and the chemical's physical properties and mechanism of action. Toxidromes reflect the net effect on autonomic and neuromuscular function: stimulated states arise from sympathetic, anticholinergic, or hallucinogen activity or from drug withdrawal; depressed states from functional sympatholytics, cholinergic agents, opioids, and sedative-hypnotic GABAergic agents; discordant states from asphyxiants, CNS syndromes, membrane-active agents, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis inducers. In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangement is secondary to depression of central cardiovascular and respiratory centers (or resulting hypoxemia) and is seen only with marked depression of consciousness, whereas direct/peripheral sympatholytics can cause prominent cardiovascular depression without comparable CNS depression. Some agents (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) owe their toxicity to metabolites more toxic than the parent compound.
additionalDifferentials: Structural CNS lesion (focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt imaging)
Sepsis or other infection causing altered mental status
Primary psychiatric illness or psychogenic illness (fear of poisoning, mass hysteria)
Metabolic encephalopathy (hepatic, renal, or respiratory failure)
infectionMimics: Sepsis with shock and multiorgan dysfunction (hypoxemia/shock from severe poisoning can mimic, and secondary aspiration pneumonia and sepsis can complicate poisoning)
nonInfectiousMimics: Psychogenic illness and anxiety reactions, which can produce mild physiologic stimulation indistinguishable from a toxic cause without observation or ancillary testing
Primary cardiac arrhythmia or conduction disease
Endocrine emergencies (e.g., thyroid storm mimicking a sympathomimetic toxidrome)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome (CNS syndromes that may overlap with stimulant toxidromes)
additionalInvestigations: Anion-gap calculation (elevated AGMA in advanced methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate poisoning, and any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures, or shock; abnormally low anion gap suggests bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, or magnesium)
Serum lactate (typically low relative to anion gap in toxic-alcohol/salicylate poisoning, high and near-equal to the gap in hypoperfusion)
Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L difference suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as a toxic alcohol or glycol)
ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation from membrane-active agents and hyperkalemia, ventricular tachyarrhythmias)

Quantitative serum levels for acetaminophen, alcohols (including ethylene glycol and methanol), anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, heavy metals, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, and methemoglobin
Qualitative urine drug screen (most useful when toxicity is severe or unexplained, e.g., coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms)

Radiography/abdominal CT (radiopaque densities suggest chloral hydrate, chlorinated hydrocarbons, heavy metals, drug packets, iodinated compounds, potassium salts, enteric-coated tablets, or salicylates; chest x-ray for pulmonary edema, metal fume fever, elemental mercury)
Review of the state Prescription Monitoring Program for controlled-substance history
PT/INR (useful for risk stratification in warfarin/rodenticide poisoning, but unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose)
redFlags: Coma or progressively decreasing level of consciousness
Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (QRS/QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias)
Hyperthermia or hypothermia (temperature elevation is the most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal states)
Suspected ingestion of a toxic time-bomb or an agent with toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol)
Body packing or body stuffing (concealment of illicit drug packets)
Intentional (suicidal) overdose requiring continuous observation and self-injury precautions
harrison.prognosis: Overall mortality is low at less than 1% of all poisoning exposures, with most being minor or non-toxic and involving children under 6 years. Mortality is substantially higher (1-2%) among hospitalized patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications from drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning. Carbon monoxide is the overall leading cause of poisoning death, although it is underrepresented in hospital and poison-center statistics because such patients are typically dead when found and referred directly to medical examiners. Drug overdose deaths have risen steadily since 1999 (over 106,600 U.S. deaths in 2021; age-adjusted rate 32.4 per 100,000), driven largely by synthetic opioids such as fentanyl and emerging agents such as xylazine. Once the offending agent is eliminated, maintaining tissue perfusion is critical to complete recovery.
pitfalls: Relying on the gag reflex as an indicator of the need for intubation; it is not reliable, and a patient may protect the airway while stimulated but not when left alone.
Treating a negative qualitative drug screen as exclusion of poisoning; the agent may be undetectable by the assay or present below the limit of detection, and repeat testing later may turn positive.
Treating a positive qualitative screen as diagnostic or forensic; cross-reacting drugs cause false positives and confirmatory GC/MS may take weeks.

Assuming blood levels correlate with toxicity during absorption/distribution (levels can exceed tissue concentrations) or during resolution (levels fall below tissue concentrations); rebound increases (e.g., lithium) can occur after extracorporeal removal stops.

Discharging too early after ingestion of a toxic time-bomb (slow-absorption, slow-distribution, metabolic-activation, or metabolism-disrupting agents) on the basis of an initially benign presentation.
Failing to consider all medications available in the home (including pet medications) when the history is unclear in a suspected poisoning.
Overlooking intentional self-harm: failing to maintain continuous observation and self-injury precautions in patients who have attempted suicide.

Using class IA, IC, or III antiarrhythmics, or beta blockers driven by sympathetic hyperactivity, for toxin-induced ventricular arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the preferred first agent for membrane-active toxicity.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression on a 1-4 scale. Stimulation: Grade 1 - anxious, irritable, tremulous with normal vital signs; Grade 2 - agitated, possible confusion/hallucinations but still able to converse and follow commands, mildly-to-moderately elevated vital signs; Grade 3 - delirious, unintelligible speech, uncontrollable motor hyperactivity, markedly raised vital signs, possible tachyarrhythmias; Grade 4 - coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression: Grade 1 - lethargic/sleeping but arousable, able to converse; Grade 2 - responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; Grade 3 - unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, decreased tone/respiration/temperature; Grade 4 - flaccid paralysis, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, decreased cardiovascular vital signs.
